_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 160 - Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, Gutenberg #66547 (1915): chs. II-X, XII, XVIII. Topics 9 sacred landscape, 5 ritual origin, 1 creation, 3 heroic. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

title.en: The Legendary Places of Ancient Kou

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 2 (New York 1915)

summary.en: A gazetteer of myth around old Honolulu: the surf Ke-kai-o-Mamala named for the chiefess Mamala; Kewalo, where the Kauwa servants were drowned and where owls would later defeat king Kakuhihewa; Punchbowl, hill of human sacrifice under the 'raging tabu fire of Keaka'; Waolani, wilderness home of the gods, where the god Kahano lay with one hand on Kahiki and one on Oahu, and over his arms the Menehune fairies crossed to build fish-ponds and temples; the magic breadfruit tree, the burial place of Maikoha, father of the wauke kapa tree, and the Canoe of the Dragon stone in the Nuuanu stream.
summary.zh: 古檀香山（庫）神話地誌：以女衝浪手瑪瑪拉得名的『瑪瑪拉之海』浪；凱瓦洛——僕隸溺亡之地，後亦為群鴉勝國王之戰場；火山彈坑山——『凱卡之烈焰禁忌』下的人祭之丘；瓦奧拉尼——眾神荒野之家，神卡哈諾一臂擱塔希提、一臂擱瓦胡，梅內胡內小矮人便沿其臂跨海而來築塘造廟；尚有魔法麵包樹、卡帕之樹的埋葬地，以及努瓦努溪中『龍之舟』聖石。

sensitivity.note: Gazetteer record consolidating place-lore; sacrifice details summarized.

passages.text: Ho-no-lu-lu is a name made by the union of the two words Hono and lulu; the old Hawaiians said Hono means abundance and lulu means calm, or peace - abundance of peace. Kakuhihewa was a king of Oahu in the long, long ago, so noted that for centuries the island has been named after him 'The Oahu of Kakuhihewa'; what is now Honolulu was almost always mentioned as Kou, after the chief Kou, an ilamuku under King Kakuhihewa. Ke-kai-o-Mamala was the name of the surf which came in the outer entrance of the harbor of Kou, named after Mamala, a chiefess who loved to play konane, drink awa, and ride the surf. Kewalo was the place where the Kauwa, a very low class of servants, were drowned by holding their heads under water, a custom known as Ke-kai-heehee, the sliding of the servants under the waves of the sea; it was also the nesting-ground of the owl who was the cause of a battle between the owls and the king Kakuhihewa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 2 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Puu-o-wai-na, or Punchbowl, was a hill of sacrifice according to the meaning of the native words. Kamakau says: 'Formerly there was an imu ahi, a fire oven, for burning men on this hill; chiefs and common people were burned as sacrifices in that noted place; people could be burned in this place for violating the tabus of the tabu divine chiefs.' Part of an ancient chant concerning Punchbowl reads: 'O the raging tabu fire of Keaka, O the high ascending fire of the sacrifice! Tabu fire, scattered ashes. Tabu fire, spreading heat.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 2 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Nuuanu Valley's most interesting legendary place is the little valley called Waolani, the wilderness home of the gods, belonging to the eepa people, almost the same as the ill-shaped gnomes of European fairy tales. In this valley was the heiau Waolani built for Ka-hanai-a-ke-Akua, the chief brought up by the gods, long before the days of Kakuhihewa. It was said that the divine caretakers of this chief were Kahano and Newa, and that Kahano was the god who lay down on the ocean stretching out his hands until one rested on Kahiki and the other rested on Oahu; over his arms as a great bridge walked the Menehunes, or fairy people, to Oahu. They came to be servants for the young chief; they built fish-ponds and temples, lived in Manoa Valley and on Punchbowl Hill, and their master Ku-leo-nui could call them any evening, his voice heard over all the island, each task finished before the rising sun drove them to their hidden resorts. Nearer the banks of the Nuuanu stream was the great bread-fruit tree into which a woman thrust her husband by magic power when he was about to be offered as sacrifice; at the foot of the valley Pu-iwa was where the father Maikoha told his daughters to bury his body, that from it might spring the wauke tree used for making kapa; and in the bed of the stream is the legendary stone called The Canoe of the Dragon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 2 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tree That Became the God of Pakaka Temple

region.zh: 瓦胡島庫帕卡卡神廟（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 3 (New York 1915)

summary.en: In Kahiki the ancestress Haumea demands a singing-flower tree as the price of saving mother and child in childbirth; the wavering princess pays at last, and Haumea plants the tree by the Wai-hee stream of Maui, where it takes root. A flood hurls it to the sea: one branch becomes the fish-gathering god Makalei, another the Maui god Ku-ke-olo-ewa, and the trunk, found rolling on the beach by a childless couple after omens, is carved as Ku-hoo-nee-nuu and enshrined at Pakaka, the most noted temple of Oahu, school of its priests for centuries.
summary.zh: 遠國卡希基，女祖豪梅亞以一株開歌聲之花的奇樹為價救活難產母女；公主三度反悔、三度復許，終於獻樹。豪梅亞攜樹渡海，種於毛伊懷希溪畔，樹遂生根。山洪暴發，樹被捲入海：一枝成為聚魚之神馬卡萊伊，一枝成毛伊庫克奧洛埃瓦，樹幹則被無嗣夫婦按夢兆於灘上拾得，雕為庫呼尼努神，供於瓦胡島最負盛名的帕卡卡神廟——百餘年來祭司學堂之所在。

sensitivity.note: God-image origin legend; healing bargain paraphrased.

passages.text: Olopana had sailed away from Waipio, Hawaii, for the islands of distant seas, and somewhere in the great number of islands grouped under the general name Kahiki found a home. Here his daughter Mu-lei-ula was experiencing great trouble being near to childbirth. For some reason Haumea, one of the divine Polynesian ancestors, had stopped for a time to visit the people of that land. When the friends were afraid that Mu-lei-ula would die, Haumea came to help, saying: 'In our land the mother lives; the mother and child both live.' She demanded as payment a beautiful tree with two strange but glorious flowers, 'the tree of changing leaves', with one kind of flower singing sharply and the other singing from time to time. Gladly the sick girl and her friends promised to give this beautiful tree to Haumea, and the chiefess rapidly grew stronger; but she repented the gift and cried, 'I will not give the tree' - and immediately began to lose strength. Twice she renounced and re-promised, and Olopana in agony cried to his daughter to give up her tree; then Haumea, with the most powerful incantations, gave her the final strength, and mother and child both lived and became well and strong.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 3 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Haumea took the tree and travelled over the far seas to Hawaii, finding no place to plant it; she crossed to Maui and came to the four rivers, where she prepared the awa of the gods but needed fresh water to mix with it. She laid her tree on the ground at Puu-kume by the Wai-hee stream and went down after water; when she returned the tree had rooted, and while she looked it began to stand up and send forth branches. She built a stone wall around it, and when it blossomed returned to her divine home in Nuumealani, the land of mists and shadows where the gods dwelt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 3 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: A man with his stone axe went out to cut a tree, perhaps to make a god, and after hours of labor cut down the new short beautiful tree. That night a fierce and mighty storm came down from the mountains; blood-red were the streams of water pouring down into the valleys. During twenty nights and twenty days the angry rain punished the land, built up hills and dug ravines, crushed the wall, scattered the stones, and bore the tree down a deep ravine; the branches were carried far out into the ocean. For six months the waves tossed this burden, and at last threw the largest branch on the reef near the beach of Kailua on Hawaii; where this branch lay stranded, fish of many kinds gathered leaping around it, and the chiefs took it inland and made the god Makalei, a god of Hawaii for generations. Another branch became the Maui god Ku-ke-olo-ewa. The body of the tree rolled back and forth along the beach; a chief and his wife who had not yet found a god for their home were led by omens down to the beach, saw a dim haze playing over it in the moonlight, took the tree, cut out their god and called it Ku-hoo-nee-nuu. They built a temple for this god, named Waihau, and made it tabu to the priests and high chiefs; the mana of this god was very great, from Hawaii to Kauai. The king living on Oahu heard about the tree, sent servants to Maui, and the chief readily gave up his god; so the temple was built at Kou and the god placed in it - this was Pakaka, the most noted temple on Oahu, and its god, the log of the tree from a foreign land, became the god of the chiefs of Oahu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 3 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Papa and the Tabu Breadfruit Tree

region.zh: 瓦胡島努瓦努谷與卡利希

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 4 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Papa (Haumea) and Wakea, the first residents of Oahu, live in the uplands by Kilohana precipice. Ruler Lele-hoo-mao's servants seize Wakea as a sacrifice for Pakaka temple. Papa overtakes the captive at the tabu breadfruit tree at Nini, and the tree opens; she leaps inside with him, passes through its other side, and hurls away her vine skirt - the morning-glory - as they escape. The cutters' chips kill all who touch them until the priest Wohi recognizes Papa from Kahiki, orders sacrifice and coconut oil, and the tree is felled into a goddess, Ka-meha-i-kana, whose image later passed to Kamehameha as a war-winning god.
summary.zh: 波利尼西亞始祖帕帕與瓦基亞定居瓦胡高地。統領萊勒呼毛奧的僕役捕瓦基亞獻祭帕卡卡廟。帕帕在尼尼的禁忌麵包樹下追上押解隊伍；古樹忽啟，她攜夫躍入樹心，自彼端破壁而出，將藤裙化作牽牛花隨手拋去。伐木者斧屑濺身即斃，祭司沃希認出此乃卡希基來的帕帕女神，命眾獻黑豬黑卡瓦紅魚、以椰油塗身，方敢伐樹——樹被雕為女神卡梅哈伊卡納，其神像後為卡美哈梅哈的開國戰神。

sensitivity.note: Variant of the Puna/Kiha-wahine breadfruit legend; cross-referenced below.

passages.text: The wonderful bread-fruit tree was a great tree growing on the eastern bank of the rippling brook Puehuehu; it was a tabu tree, set apart for the high chief from Kou and the chiefs from Honolulu to rest under while on their way to bathe in the celebrated diving-pool Wai-kaha-lulu. That tree became a god. Papa and Wakea were the ancestors of the great scattered sea-going people living in all the islands now known as Polynesia; they came to the island of Oahu, and according to almost all the legends were the first residents. Papa was a kupua - a woman having many wonderful and miraculous powers - sometimes called Haumea, but at last she left her power and a new name, Ka-meha-i-kana, in the magic bread-fruit tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 4 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the Honolulu side of the mountains were many chiefs, among them Lele-hoo-mao, the ruler, whose fields were often despoiled by Papa and her husband; it was his servants who, searching the country around these fields, had found and captured Wakea, forcing him toward the temple Pakaka to be offered in sacrifice, shouting, 'We have found the mischief-maker and have tied him.' Papa threw around her some of the vines she had fashioned into a skirt and ran over the hills to the edge of Nuuanu Valley; a man by the stream told her a man had been carried by who was to be baked in an oven that day. She took a stone and smashed it against the ground, breaking through into a pool of water, drank and hastened on to the bread-fruit tree at Nini, where she overtook her husband and the men who guarded him. Wailing that she must kiss him, she rushed to him and began pushing and pulling him, whirling him around and around. Suddenly the great bread-fruit tree opened and she leaped with him through the doorway into the heart of the tree; the opening closed in a moment. By her miraculous power she opened the tree on the other side, and they passed through and went rapidly up the mountain-side. As they ran, Papa threw off her vine pa-u; the vine became the beautiful morning-glory, delicate in blossom and powerful in medicinal qualities. The astonished men had lost their captive; as the ancient proverb says, 'Their fence was around the field of nothingness.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 4 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chiefs consulted together and decided to cut down the tree and take the captive out of his hiding-place. The leader of the tree-cutters struck the tree with his stone axe; a chip leaped from the tree, struck him, and he fell dead. Another caught the axe - again chips flew and the workman fell dead. Whenever a chip hit any one he died, and the sap of the tree flowed out and was spattered under the blows of the stone axes; whenever a drop touched a workman or a bystander he fell dead. The people were filled with fear and cried to their priest for help. Wohi, the priest, came to the tree, bowed before it and remained in silent thought a long time, then raised his head and said: 'It was not a woman who went into that tree. It was Papa from Kahiki. She is a goddess and has a multitude of bodies. If we treat her well we shall not be destroyed.' He commanded the people to offer sacrifices at the foot of the tree - a black pig, black awa and red fish - then to rub themselves bountifully with coconut oil and go fearlessly to their work; chips struck them and the sap was spattered over them, but they toiled on unhurt until the great tree fell. Out of this magic bread-fruit tree a great goddess was made. Papa gave to it one of her names, Ka-meha-i-kana, and endowed it with power so that it was noted from Kauai to Hawaii; it became one of the great gods of Oahu, but was taken to Maui, where Kamehameha secured it as his god to aid in establishing his rule over all the islands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 4 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: After a time Papa had a daughter, Kapo, who also had kupua power; Kapo had many names, such as Kapo-ula-kinau and Laka, and was a high tabu goddess of the ancient Hawaiian hulas, having the power of assuming many bodies at will, from the mo-o, or lizard, to a human being. Kapo was born from the eyes of Haumea, or Papa. Papa looked away from Kapo and there was born from her head a sharp pali, often mist-covered - this was Ka-moho-alii. Then Pele was born, the one who had mighty battles with Kamapuaa, the pig-man, who almost destroyed the volcano Kilauea; it was Ka-moho-alii who rubbed sticks and rekindled the volcanic fires for his sister Pele, thus driving Kamapuaa down the sides of Kilauea into the ocean. These three, according to the Honolulu legends, were the highest-born children of Papa and Wakea. Down the Kalihi stream below Papa's home were two stones to which the Hawaiians gave eepa power: if a traveller passes, he stops, gathers leaves, makes leis and places them on these stones, that there may be no trouble in all that day's wanderings - hence the proverb of Kalihi Valley, 'Here is the sharp-headed rain of Kalihi.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 4 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Kane and Kanaloa Strike Springs from the Rock
title.zh: 卡內與卡納洛亞擊石得泉

region.zh: 瓦胡島卡利希與馬諾阿谷

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 5 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Four great gods come from Kahiki to Nuuanu Valley: Ku, Lono, Ka-ne and Kanaloa. Kane and Kanaloa are the water-finders, each pool a Ka-Wai-a-ke-Akua. Walking Kauai unheeded as men, they drink awa from coast to coast; at Kalihi Kane smashes his great staff into the lava bed and water leaps up - the water-door of Kalihi; in Manoa Valley he splits the precipice for the pool still called the Water Provided by a God, whose bearers cried their warning and made all fall prostrate before Kamehameha's royal drink.
summary.zh: 四大神自卡希基來到努瓦努谷：庫、龍諾、卡內與卡納洛亞。卡內與卡納洛亞是尋水之神，凡泉池皆稱『神賜之水』。二人如凡人般走遍考愛島無人禮拜，便一路啜卡瓦酒至瓦胡。卡利希處，卡內以巨杖猛擊熔岩，清泉迸湧——『卡利希水門』；馬諾阿谷中，他劈開崖壁成潭，至今猶名『神賜之水』。卡美哈梅哈王時代，取水使者沿途高呼，行人皆伏身於王之神飲之前。

sensitivity.note: Westervelt explicitly notes the motif is not Biblical-derived.

passages.text: Four great gods with a large retinue of lesser gods came from Kahiki to the Hawaiian Islands: Ku, Lono, Ka-ne and Kanaloa. Ka-ne and Kanaloa were the water-finders, opening springs and pools over all the islands, each pool known as Ka-Wai-a-ke-Akua, the water provided by a god. In one of the very old Hawaiian newspapers the question was asked, 'What are the waters of Ka-ne?' and the answers came: the heavy showers of life-giving rain, the mountain stream swelling into a torrent, the rainbow-colored rain loved by Ka-ne, the continually flowing brooks of the valleys - these were the waters of Ka-ne. Prayers were offered to the two gods in all the different stages of farming, with the prayer, 'Here is food, O Gods, Ka-ne and Kanaloa! Give life to us and our family, life for the parents feeble with age, life for all in the household, when digging and planting our land; this is our prayer. Amama.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 5 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ka-ne and Kanaloa were great travellers. Together they journeyed over Kauai, coming from far-away lands; they appeared more like men than gods, and the Kauai people did not worship them, so they opened up only a few springs and crossed over to Oahu. Throughout all the islands the awa root has been found, bitter and very astringent, but when crushed and mixed with water the juice became a liquor greatly loved - 'These two gods drank awa from Kauai to Hawaii', so the old legends say. At Kalihi a number of fine awa roots were growing; they pulled up the roots and prepared them for chewing. When the awa was ready Kanaloa looked for fresh water but could not find any, and said to Ka-ne, 'Our awa is good, but there is no water in this place. Where can we find water for this awa?' Ka-ne said, 'There is indeed water here.' He had a large and strong staff, in some of the legends called a spear; he began to strike the earth, deep went the point into the rock, smashing and splintering it and breaking open a hole out of which water leaped for them to mix with their prepared awa. This pool has been known since the days of old as Ka-puka-Wai-o-Kalihi, the water door of Kalihi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 5 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: They passed Nuuanu Valley and went into Manoa Valley, the home of the rainbow princess. There the gods found most excellent awa, and Kanaloa cried, 'O my brother, this is awa surpassing any other we have found; but where shall I go to find water?' Ka-ne replied, 'Here in this hillside is water.' So he took his staff and struck it fiercely against the precipice; rapidly the rocks were broken off, the precipice crept back from the mighty strokes of the god, and a large pool of clear, cool water appeared among the great stones which had fallen. There they mixed awa and water and drank again and again until the sleep of the drunkard came. This pool is still at the head of Manoa Valley, called Ka-Wai-a-ke-Akua, the water provided by a god. In the days of Kamehameha I very often messengers came from this pool with calabashes full of water swinging from the ends of sticks laid over their shoulders; when they came near any individual or group of Hawaiians they had to call out loudly, giving warning so that all by whom they passed could fall prostrate before the gift of the gods to the great king. Kane and Kanaloa made many springs of fresh water in all the different islands, and went to Kohala, Hawaii, where they lived in a temple so long that the people thought they were gods and offered sacrifices and worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 5 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: The Quest for the Water of Life of Ka-ne

region.en: Sorcerer-king's palace in the far lands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 遠國巫王之宮（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 6 (New York 1915)

summary.en: A dying king's three sons seek the water of life of Ka-ne, which restores the dead and makes the old young again. Two rough sons push aside the dwarf who bars the path and are strangled in living vines; the youngest speaks gently, receives a strong staff and three bundles of food, strikes the sorcerer's wall thrice, feeds the two dragons at its fountain, and fills his calabash at midnight. Betrayed by jealous brothers who swap the water for sea-salt, he is exiled, until three grateful kings tell his father the truth - and the maiden of Kane's palace walks straight to him along her line in the air.
summary.zh: 老王垂危，三子奉命尋取卡內的生命之水——它能起死回生、返老還童。兩位粗暴的兄長推開守路的侏儒，被活藤縛斃於林中；幼子溫言求助，獲神杖與三束祭食，三擊破巫王之牆，以食飼雙龍，午夜前灌滿葫蘆。歸途兄弟以鹹海水偷換聖水，父王反被毒害，幼子蒙冤流放；直至三國君王攜禮來謝、真相大白——而卡內宮中的公主沿著空中劃線直奔他而來，選他為夫。

sensitivity.note: Water-of-life cluster: ATU 551-type tale in Hawaiian dress.

passages.text: When the moon dies she goes to the living water of Ka-ne, to the water which can restore all to life, even the moon to the path in the sky - so runs the Maori legend. The Hawaiians of long ago shared the belief that somewhere along the deep sea beyond the horizon, or somewhere in the cloud-land above the heavens, there was a land known as the land of the water of life of the gods, in which was a lake of living water in which always rested the power of restoration to life - Ka wai ola a Ka-ne. Mention of this wai ola is found in New Zealand, the Tongas, Samoa, Tahiti and the Hawaiian Islands. Ka-ne was one of the four greatest gods of the Polynesians; in his hands was placed the care of the water of life; a sick person drinking it would recover health, and a dead person sprinkled with it would be restored to life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the misty past a king was very, very ill, and all his friends thought he was going to die. An old man, a stranger, passing by the three wailing sons said slowly: 'I have heard of something which would make your father well. He must drink of the water of life of Ka-ne. But this is very hard to find and difficult to get.' The eldest son ran to his father for permission, and as he went along a path through the forest, suddenly an ugly little man, a dwarf, appeared in his path and called out, 'Where are you going that you are in such a hurry?' The prince answered roughly, pushed the little man aside and ran on; the dwarf made the path twist and turn and grow narrow, until the prince fell, crawling and fighting against tangled masses of ferns and clinging tendrils of the vines of the land of fairies and gnomes; they twined around him and tied him tight with living coils, and he lay like one who was dead. The second son, thinking the selfish thought that he might win the kingdom, met the same little man, spoke roughly, pushed him out of the way, and was caught in the tangled woods and held fast like one who was dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the last, the youngest son, took his calabash and went away thinking he might be able to rescue his brothers as well as get the water of life for his father. He told the dwarf about the king's illness and the report of the water of life of Ka-ne, and asked if he could aid in any way. The little man said, 'Because you have spoken gently and have asked my help and have not been rough and rude as were your brothers, I will tell you where to go and will give you aid. The path will open before you at the bidding of this strong staff which I give you. You will come to the palace of a king who is a sorcerer; in his house is the fountain of that water of life. Take three bundles of food in one hand and your strong staff in the other; strike the door of that king's house three times and an opening will be made. Then you will see two dragons with open mouths ready to devour you; quickly throw food in their mouths and they will become quiet. Fill your calabash with the living water and hurry away. At midnight the doors will be shut, and you cannot escape.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The prince came to the strange land and the sorcerer's house; three times he struck until he broke the wall and made a door for himself. He saw the dragons and threw the food into their mouths, making them his friends. He saw some young chiefs, who welcomed him and gave him a war-club and a bundle of food; in another room he met a beautiful maiden whom he loved at once with all his heart, who told him that after a time they would meet again and live as husband and wife, and showed him where he could get the water of life. He dipped his calabash in the spring and leaped through the door just at the stroke of midnight. He found his brothers in the tangled path and sprinkled a little of the water of life over them, so that strength returned; but they were jealous and angry at the success of their younger brother. They passed lands where the high chief was resisting rebels; the young prince gave them part of the bundle of food from the house of the god Ka-ne, and they ate and became very strong, and the war-club destroyed the rebels. At the seacoast of their own land the wicked brothers took his calabash of the water of life and poured the water into their water-jars, filling his calabash with salt, sickish sea-water. The king drank deeply of the salt water and was made more seriously sick, almost to death; then the older brothers gave him the real water of life and he immediately became strong as in the days of his youth. The king was very angry with the youngest son and sent him away with an officer, a friend who helped him find a safe hiding-place. By and by three great kings came from distant lands with presents for the prince who had given them peace and prosperity; the father acknowledged the wrong he had done. Meanwhile one of the most beautiful princesses of all the world had sent word everywhere that she would be seated in her house and any prince who could walk straight to her along a line drawn in the air by her sorcerers, without turning to either side, should be her husband. The brothers had both failed, but the young prince went with swift steps of love straight to a door which opened of its own accord; out leaped the maiden of the palace of the land of Ka-ne, and into his arms she rushed. The brothers ran away to distant lands and never returned; the prince and the princess became king and queen and lived in great peace and happiness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 6 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Mamala Rides the Sea of Kou

region.zh: 瓦胡島檀香山庫港入口

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 7 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Mamala, a kupua chiefess - great lizard, shark and beautiful woman in one - dances on the roughest outer waves of the harbor entrance whose surf still bears her name. Leaving her shark-man husband Ouha for the chief Hono-kau-pu, she drives him away; humiliated when the shrimps in his offered basket leap back to the sea amid the women's taunts, Ouha casts off humanity and becomes the great shark-god of the coast between Waikiki and Koko Head, while the mele of Hono-kau-pu keeps her riding 'from the top of the tossing surf waves'.
summary.zh: 瑪瑪拉是庫普阿族女酋——巨蜥、鯊與絕色美人三位一體——於港口外最洶湧的浪頭上翩然起舞，港之浪濤至今仍冠其名。她離開鯊人丈夫烏哈改嫁霍諾考普；烏哈獻蝦求恕，蝦群躍水而逃，遭婦人嘲笑；他拋卻人身，化為威基基與科科角之間海岸的大鯊神。霍諾考普的古歌至今傳唱：『我自濤尖盼君歸——今夜，庫港的雙眼終得相會。』

passages.text: Kou was a noted place for games and sports among the chiefs of long ago. Straight out toward the ocean was the narrow entrance to the harbor, through which rolled the finest surf waves of old Honolulu; the surf bore the name Ke-kai-o-Mamala, the sea of Mamala, and when it rose high it was called Ka-nuku-o-Mamala, the nose of Mamala. Mamala was a chiefess of kupua character: she was a mo-o, a gigantic lizard or crocodile, as well as a beautiful woman, and could assume whichever shape she most desired; one of the legends says that she was a shark and woman. She had for her first husband the shark-man Ouha, afterward a shark-god having his home in the ocean near Koko Head; Mamala and Ouha drank awa together and played konane on the large smooth stone at Kou.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 7 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mamala was a wonderful surf-rider; very skilfully she danced on the roughest waves. The surf in which she most delighted rose far out in the rough sea, where the winds blew strong and whitecaps rolled in rough disorder into the bay of Kou; the people on the beach, watching her, filled the air with resounding applause, clapping their hands over her extraordinary athletic feats. The chief Hono-kau-pu chose to take Mamala as his wife, so she left Ouha and lived with her new husband. Ouha was angry and tried at first to injure Hono and Mamala, but he was driven away; he fled to the lake Ka-ihi-Kapu toward Waikiki, where he appeared as a man with a basketful of shrimps and fresh fish, which he offered to the women of that place, saying, 'Here is life for the children.' He opened his basket, but the shrimps and the fish leaped out and escaped into the water. The women ridiculed the god-man; as the ancient legendary characters of all Polynesia could not endure anything that brought shame or disgrace upon them in the eyes of others, Ouha fled from the taunts of the women, casting off his human form and dissolving his connection with humanity - thus he became the great shark-god of the coast between Waikiki and Koko Head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 7 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The surf-rider was remembered in the beautiful mele coming from ancient times and called the mele of Hono-kau-pu: 'The surf rises at Koolau, blowing the waves into mist, into little drops, spray falling along the hidden harbor. There is my dear husband Ouha, there is the shaking sea, the running sea of Kou, the crab-like moving sea of Kou. Prepare the awa to drink, the crab to eat; the small konane board is at Hono-kau-pu. My friend on the highest point of the surf: this is a good surf for us. My love has gone away. Smooth is the floor of Kou, fine is the breeze from the mountains. I wait for you to return; the games are prepared. Leap away to Tahiti by the path to Nuumealani, home of the gods - will that lover return? I belong to Hono-kau-pu, from the top of the tossing surf waves; the eyes of the day and the night are forgotten. Kou has the large konane board; this is the day, and to-night the eyes meet at Kou.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 7 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Ka-ehu Pushes the Man-eater Pehu into the Shallows
title.zh: 卡埃胡智懲食人鯊佩胡

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 8 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Ka-ehu, the little yellow shark of Pearl Harbor gifted with wisdom by the shark-god Ka-moho-alii, pines for his home in Puna and sets out for Hawaii. At Waikiki he meets Pehu, a man-eating shark from Maui, 'catching a crab' for breakfast among the surf-riders. Pretending to help, Ka-ehu stations Pehu by the reef, signals his sharks at the right wave, shoves the surfers aside, and tosses the leaping Pehu head-first into a deep coral hole; the surf-riders kill him and find hair and bones inside - proof of his meals - and burn the pieces in a great oven at Pele-ula.
summary.zh: 珍珠港的小黃鯊卡埃胡蒙鯊神卡莫霍阿利賜予智慧，思鄉而返夏威夷。途經威基基，遇毛伊來的食人鯊佩胡在衝浪者間『捉蟹當早餐』。卡埃胡假意相助，令其藏身礁影，並約定：浪頭來時群鯊齊發。時機一到，衝浪者被推至一側，躍起撲食的佩胡被眾鯊拋得團團轉，頭朝下栽進深珊瑚洞；衝浪者合力誅之，剖腹見髮見骨——皆其食人罪證——碎屍於佩雷烏拉大灶焚化。

passages.text: Among the legendary characters of the early Hawaiians was Ka-ehu, the little yellow shark of Pearl Harbor, who had been given magic power and great wisdom by his ancestor Ka-moho-alii, the shark-god, brother of the fire goddess Pele. Part of his life had been spent with his parents, who guarded the sea precipices of the Coast of Puna in the southern part of the island Hawaii. While at Pearl Harbor he became homesick for the beauty of Puna, and chanted: 'O my land of rustling lehua-trees! Rain is treading on your budding flowers; they meet the fish in the sea. This is the day when love meets love; my longings are stirring within me for the spirit friends of my land. They call me back to my home; I must return.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 8 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ka-ehu called his shark friends and started along the Oahu shores on his way to Hawaii. At Waikiki they met Pehu, a shark visitor from Maui, who lived in the sea belonging to Hono-ka-hau; Pehu was a man-eating shark, swimming back and forth at Kalehua-wike waiting for some surf-rider to go out far enough to be caught. Ka-ehu asked him what he was doing there; he replied, 'I am catching a crab for my breakfast.' Ka-ehu said, 'We will help you catch your crab', and told Pehu to go near the coral reef while he and his large retinue of sharks would go seaward: when a number of surf-riders were far out they would appear and drive them shoreward in a tumultuous rush, and then Pehu could easily catch the crab. This pleased the shark from Maui, so he went close to the reef and hid himself in its shadows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 8 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ka-ehu said to his friends: 'We must kill this man-eating shark who is destroying our people. This will be a part of our pay to them for honoring us at Puu-loa, Pearl Harbor; we will all go and push Pehu into the shallow water.' A number of surf-riders poised on the waves, and Pehu called for the other sharks to come, but Ka-ehu told him to wait for a better chance. Soon two men started on a wave from the distant dark blue sea where the high surf begins. Ka-ehu gave a signal for an attack: his friends were to rush in under the great wave and, as it passed over the waiting Pehu, crowd the men and their surf-boards to one side and push the leaping Pehu so that he would be upset; then, while he was floundering in the surf, they must hurl him over the reef. As Pehu leaped to catch one of the coming surf-riders he was astonished to see the man shoved to one side, then as he rose almost straight up in the water he was caught by the other sharks and tossed over and over until he plunged head first into a deep hole in the coral; he thrashed his great tail about, but only forced himself farther in so that he could not escape. The surf-riders went out to the hole and killed him and cut his body in pieces; inside the body they found hair and bones, showing that this shark had been destroying some of their people. They took the pieces to Pele-ula, where they made a great oven and burned them. Ka-ehu passed on toward Hawaii as a knight-errant, meeting many adventures and punishing evil-minded residents of the great sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 8 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Maikoha and the Birth of Kapa
title.zh: 邁科哈與樹皮布之誕生

region.zh: 瓦胡島努瓦努谷普伊瓦

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 9 (New York 1915)

summary.en: In the days before kapa the oldest clothes were dried banana leaves and ti-leaf cloaks. The farmer Maikoha of Pu-iwa, dying, bids his daughters bury him by the stream: a tree will grow from the grave, its bark for kapa. The wauke springs up; the daughters pound its bark into the first beaten cloth, and every broken branch takes root and spreads island to island. Maikoha becomes the ancestor-god of kapa-makers, his daughters the gods of pounding and of patterned beaters, Ehu the dyer's god - and Hina, mother of Maui, beats her kapa in the sky, where thunder is her rolling stones and lightning the flash between cloud-sheets.
summary.zh: 樹皮布問世之前，先民以乾蕉葉、露兜葉蔽體。普伊瓦農夫邁科哈臨終囑女兒將其葬於溪畔：墳上將生一樹，樹皮可製卡帕。瓦烏凱樹應聲而出；女兒們搗樹皮成最初的『捶打之物』，斷枝隨處生根，由島及島。邁科哈成為樹皮布匠的祖先神，二女分司搶打與花紋，染師敬染神埃胡——而毛伊之母希娜在天上捶打雲布：雷是她滾落的鎮布石，電是雲層間躍動的日光。

sensitivity.note: Craft-origin myth; technical details of kapa-making summarized.

passages.text: The old people said that in the very long ago their ancestors did not have anything like the kapa cloth which has been known for many centuries; there was no kapa maoli - nothing in nature which provided clothing or covering. The clothing of the oldest time was sometimes made by tying dried banana leaves around the body; the long fragrant leaves of the ti plant were dried, soaked in water until soft, then fastened together by braiding, making a very warm cloak worn by bird-catchers to shed rain and keep out cold. For many generations the Hawaiians made most beautiful and costly feather garments, braiding a foundation mesh of fine vegetable fibres and covering it with the most brilliant red and golden feathers from the birds of the forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 9 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: This was the valley supposed to have been the first habitation of the gods, from which all life spread over the island group; here the gnomes, or eepa people, had their home, and here the Menehunes built a temple for the child adopted by the gods. At Pu-iwa, by the side of the running water, a farmer by the name of Maikoha lived with his daughters. Years passed by and Maikoha became weak and ill; on his death-bed he called his daughters and commanded them to listen carefully and obey his words, saying: 'When I die, bury my body close to the waters of our pleasant stream. A tree will grow from that burial-place. This tree will be to you for kapa, from which you will make all things good for clothing as well as covering when you sleep or are ill. The bark of this tree is the part you will use.' When death came, the daughters buried their father by the running water, and after a time a tree grew from the grave - not tall and large, but throwing out a number of small, spreading branches. This was the wauke tree. The daughters believed it was a gift from the aumakua, the ghost-god into which the spirit of their father had been changed; reverently they touched the tree, broke off some branches, stripped off the bark, and pounded and pounded until the pieces were fastened together in a rude kind of cloth - thus they found kapa, the beaten thing, and learned how to make it into small and large pieces and to fashion such clothing as met their need.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 9 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wherever they cut or broke the branches of this new tree the broken pieces took root, or, caught by the swift-flowing stream, were tossed on the bank or carried and scattered over the plain, until they grew even to the sea; branches were carried to the other islands, thus the wauke became a blessing to all the people - this tree under the name aute, which is the same as wauke, was a blessing to many Polynesians from Tahiti to New Zealand. Maikoha became the chief aumakua, or ancestor-god, of the Hawaiian kapa-makers, and has been worshipped for generations: when they planted the wauke branches prayers, incantations and sacrifices were offered to Maikoha. One of his daughters, Lau-hu-iki, became the aumakua of all those who pounded the prepared bark; the other, Laa-hana, was worshipped by those who used especially marked clubs while beating the bark into patterns, for she learned how to scratch the clubs with sharks' teeth so that marks would be left in the pounded sheets. Ehu was made the aumakua of kapa-dyers because he learned how to dip the cloth in dyes and give it color, discovering the red dye in the blood of the kukui tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 9 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the early time a flat stone was used upon which to pound out the sheets of kapa, but blocks of wood and long heavy sticks - called kua-kuku - gave the best results, giving back a soft sound with the rhythmic beat of the mallets, accompanied by the makers' own chants and incantations to Maikoha or one of the other aumakuas. Hina, the mother of the demi-god Maui, was the great kapa-maker of the legends of the ancient Hawaiians: it is said that she still spreads her kapas in the sky - they are the beautiful clouds of all colors, sometimes piled up and sometimes lying in sheets. When fierce winds blow and lift and toss the cloud kapas and roll off the stones which Hina has placed on them to hold them down, or when she throws off the stones herself, the noise of the rolling stones is the thunder which men hear; and when Hina rolls the cloud sheets together, the folds glisten and flash in the light of the sun - thus what men call lightning is the sunlight leaping from sheet to sheet of Hina's kapas in cloudland.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 9 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Kamakau's Creation of the First Man

region.zh: 瓦胡島莫卡普小島（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Hawaiian tradition recorded by Kamakau c. 1860s; retold 1915 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 10 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Kamakau's native-history version: the earth is a calabash, its cover the sky, sun and moon of its flesh, stars of its seeds. On Mokapu Kane kneads red dirt into the form of a man; Kanaloa's mockery of dirt lacks life and is turned to stone. Ku and Lono push a spirit of the air into the image, and Kane calls it alive - 'Hiki au, E-ola!' - and the man Wela-ahi-lani-nui stands. Sleeping, he is opened and a woman taken from his body: his shadow, aka, changed into 'The-heaven-changed-shadow', Ke-aka-huli-lani, ancestress of Hawaiians and all the peoples of the great ocean.
summary.zh: 卡馬考所記：大地如葫蘆，葫蓋化天，日月出其肉，星辰出其籽。莫卡普島上，卡內以紅土捏成人形；卡納洛亞嘲弄仿製的泥像無生氣，被咒為石。庫與龍諾將空中之靈推入泥像，卡內呼曰『我來，活吧！活吧！』——巨人韋拉阿希拉尼努伊應聲而起。他熟睡之際，諸神剖其身取出一女子：那便是曾隨他左右的名為『影子』的東西，如今名為『天變之影』——夏威夷人與大洋諸島萬民之祖。

sensitivity.note: Westervelt notes part of this Kamakau account is thoroughly Biblical; kept as recorded tradition with that caveat. Humans-molded-from-clay cluster.

passages.text: Ku, Ka-ne, Lono and Kanaloa were the first gods made. The gods had come from far-off unknown lands; they brought with them the mysterious people who live in precipices and trees and rocks - the invisible spirits of the air. The earth was a calabash; the gods threw the calabash cover upward and it became the sky; part of the thick flesh became the sun, another part was the moon, and the stars came from the seeds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 10 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The gods went over to a small island called Mokapu, and thought they would make man to be chief over all other things. Mololani was the crater hill which forms the little island; on the sunrise side of this hill, near the sea, was the place where red dirt lay mixed with dark blue and black soil. Here Ka-ne scratched the dirt together and made the form of a man. Kanaloa ridiculed the mass of dirt and made a better form, but it did not have life. Ka-ne said, 'You have made a dirt image; let it become stone.' Then Ka-ne ordered Ku and Lono to carefully obey his directions; they were afraid he would kill them, so at once they caught one of the spirits of the air and pushed it into the image Ka-ne had made. When the spirit had been pushed into the body, Ka-ne stood by the image and called, 'Hiki au, E-ola! E-ola!' - I come, live! live! Ku and Lono responded 'Live! live!' Then Ka-ne called again, 'I come, awake! awake!' and the other two responded, and the image became a living man. Then Ka-ne cried, 'I come, arise! arise!' and the image stood up - a man with a living spirit. They named him Wela-ahi-lani-nui, the great heaven burning hot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 10 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The gods took this man to their home and nourished him. When he became strong he went out to walk around the home of the gods; soon he noticed a shadow going around with his body - it walked when he walked, and rested when he rested. He wondered what this thing was, and called it aka, shadow. When he slept, Ku, Ka-ne and Lono tore open his body, and Ka-ne took out a woman, leaving Ku and Lono to heal the body; then they put the woman by the side of the man and they were alike. Wela-ahi-lani-nui woke and found a beautiful one lying by him, and thought: 'This is that thing which has been by my side, my aka. The gods have changed it into this beautiful one.' So he gave her the name Ke-aka-huli-lani, the heaven-changed-shadow. These were the ancestors of the Hawaiians and all the peoples of the islands of the great ocean. It must be remembered that there are many other Hawaiian legends which mention other first men and women as ancestors of the Hawaiian people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 10 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: Ku-ilio-loa, the Great Dog of the Clouds

region.zh: 瓦胡島山穴（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 12 (New York 1915)

summary.en: The dog-god Ku-ilio-loa follows three rainbows to the bathing-pool of the chief's daughter Na-pihe-nui as a little white dog; discovered, he demands her in marriage and, refused, devours the chief's people one by one - sometimes falling like lightning on a group and striking far away almost instantly. Hidden women withstand the siege in a cave; in a final terrific battle Ku is overpowered, cut in two, and the priest's power turns the halves into two great stones. He still stretches from peak to peak among the changing clouds of Oahu - the nature-myth of the dog-shaped cloud.
summary.zh: 犬神庫伊利洛阿循三道彩虹而至酋長之女沐浴池畔，化身小白犬；被識破後索婚不遂，遂逐個吞食族人，時如閃電擊群、瞬息遠襲。酋長將婦孺藏於洞穴死守；決戰中巨犬力竭，身被斬為兩半，祭司施法使其化作兩塊巨石。至今它仍橫亙瓦胡群峰之間，隱現於變幻雲影——犬形雲的自然神話。

sensitivity.note: Cannibalism summarized; nature-myth reading per Westervelt.

passages.text: Ku, the dog-man, decided to come down from the clouds and visit mankind, so he assumed the form of a little dog and went around almost unnoticed. Ku saw a group of three rainbows moving from place to place or resting for a long time above the home of a high chief: sometimes the rainbows went up to the forests of ohia and kukui-trees, sometimes they rested over the deep pools made by the waterfalls of the swiftly descending mountain streams, and most frequently the beautiful colors were arched over a small grove of trees around a bathing-pool. Here Na-pihe-nui, the daughter of the high chief, came daily with her company of maidens to bathe and sport in the water. One day one of the girls saw something moving on the shore; they hastened to the place where their clothes had been thrown down and found a little white dog lying on the kapa mantle of the princess. For a time they played with the little stranger, delighted with his unusual intelligence, and took him with them and cared for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: The high chief Polihale was interested in the peculiar powers possessed by this strange dog; his suspicions were aroused and the dog was watched. Soon the chief learned that this was a man of marvellous ability who could appear as a dog or a man at his own pleasure, and ordered his retainers to kill the dog; it dashed into the woods and made its escape. It was the great dog Ku, who had seen the three rainbows and followed them to the bathing-pool and then, having seen the princess, had determined to carry her away as his wife. Then Ku changed himself into a man of fine appearance and came boldly to the high chief's home demanding the princess in marriage, but the chief, warned by the omens studied by his soothsayers, refused. Ku was in great anger and threatened to kill the chief's people, but the high chief drove him away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: A dream came to the high chief in which he saw the strange man coming as a great dog, stretching itself out of a cave on the mountain-side; he knew this dog with magical powers would be a very difficult enemy to overcome. The chief soon learned that Ku was catching his people one by one and devouring them, and decided to take final issue with his enemy. He hid all the women of his family in a cave, placing the princess in their care with provisions for a long siege, water found in the cave itself, and stones placed before the opening. Then the high chief and his followers waged war against Ku, the dog-man, but Ku was very strong and overthrew his pursuers; many times he killed some of the chief's people and carried their bodies away to feast upon them, and he was so swift that sometimes he fell like a flash of lightning upon a group of his foes and in an incredibly short time would make an attack in a far distant place. The high chief offered sacrifices to his gods and secured charms from his priests; incantations and prayers were prepared against Ku. At last a terrific battle was fought and Ku was overpowered and beaten to the ground; still he fought fiercely, but the hard wooden spears pierced him and the heavy clubs broke his bones, until he lay a crushed and bleeding mass at the feet of his conquerors. They cut his body in two pieces, throwing one to one side and the other to a place some distance away; then the power of the priests was invoked and the two parts of the body of Ku-ilio-loa became two great stones which have been objects of veneration among the Hawaiians for many years. Ku stretches his form along the mountains and sometimes reveals himself as the great dog among the myriad shapes which the changing clouds are ever assuming - sometimes in the clouds of Oahu, and then again his form is in the skies of other islands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 12 (1915); not verbatim.

title.en: The Battle of the Owls of Kakuhihewa
title.zh: 卡庫希黑瓦王與群鴞之戰

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 18 (New York 1915)

summary.en: Kapoi, moved by an owl's plea, gives back her seven stolen eggs, adopts her as his family god, builds her a temple at Manoa and lifts his own tabu - death under king Kakuhihewa's decree. In Waikiki's heiau the owl-king of Manoa calls the owls of every island by drum: in one day Hawaii, Lanai, Maui and Molokai's owls gather at Kalapueo, Oahu's at Kanoniakapueo, Kauai and Niihau's at Pueo-hulu-nui. At daybreak the sky is covered; owls tear eyes and faces, befoul the warriors, and Kapoi is freed - 'Your god has mana greater than my god; your god is a true god.'
summary.zh: 卡波伊為鴞之哀求所動，歸還其七枚卵，奉其為家神，於馬諾阿為之建廟，並自設又自解禁忌——依卡庫希黑瓦王之法，此乃死罪。囚於威基基神廟之際，馬諾阿的鴞王擊鼓召集各島之鴞：一日之內，夏威夷、拉奈、毛伊、摩洛凱之鴞集於卡拉普埃奧，考愛與尼豪之鴞集於普埃霍胡魯努伊。破曉時分，天空盡為鴞翼所蔽；它們啄眼撲面、污及眾武士，卡波伊得釋——王亦承認：『你的神法力高於我的神，你的神是真神。』

sensitivity.note: Owl-worship origin legend; also covers the Pueo trials establishing proof before punishment.

passages.text: Pueo, the owl-god, was also Pueo-alii, king of owls; he had kahunas who consulted him by signs, and the aumakuas, or ghost gods, sometimes in oracles. From his own residence on Owl's Hill he governed all Manoa Valley. It was said that one of the natives in the valley displeased him; he captured the man and at once ordered the death penalty, calling him a rebel. The man secured the attention of the owl-god for a moment and presented the plea that he ought to be permitted to say something for himself before he was punished; the execution was delayed, the man proved that he was innocent of the charge against him, and the owl-god established a law that a person must be proved guilty before he could be condemned and punished. This came to be a custom among the Hawaiians as the years passed by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Down Pauoa Valley dashes a stream of beautiful clear water, passing the eastern edge of Punchbowl Hill. Here at Kahehuna lived a man by the name of Kapoi, whose grass house was decaying, its thatch falling to pieces. Kapoi went to the Kewalo marsh near the beach, where tall pili grass was growing, to get a bundle for thatching; he found a nest of owl's eggs, took up his bundle of grass and the nest and returned home. In the evening he prepared to cook the eggs, making a fire in his small imu with his fire-sticks; an owl flew down and sat on the wall by the gate. Kapoi had almost finished wrapping the eggs in ti leaves and was about to lay them on the hot stones when the owl called to him: 'O Kapoi! Give me my eggs.' 'How many eggs belong to you?' 'I have seven eggs.' 'I am cooking these eggs for I have no fish.' 'O Kapoi! You are heartless, and you have no sorrow for me if you do not give back my eggs.' Kapoi was touched, and said, 'Come and get your eggs.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: Because of this kindness the owl became Kapoi's god, and commanded him to build a heiau and make a raised place and an altar for sacrifice at Manoa. He laid a sacrifice and some bananas on the altar, established the day for the tabu to begin and the day when the tabu should be lifted. This was talked about by the people, and by and by the high chief heard that a man had built a temple for his god, had made it tabu and had lifted the tabu. Kakuhihewa was living at Waikiki, the king after whom the island Oahu was named Oahu-a-Kakuhihewa; he had made a law for the temple he was building at Waikiki, decreeing that if any chief or man should build a temple with a tabu on it and should lift that tabu before the tabu on the king's temple should be over, that chief or man should pay the penalty of death as a rebel. The king sent out his servants and captured Kapoi; they brought him to Waikiki and placed him in the king's heiau Kapalaha, where he was to be killed and offered in sacrifice to the offended god of the king's temple.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.

passages.text: His owl-god was grateful for the return of the eggs and determined to reward him for his kindness and protect him as a worshipper. This owl-god was a family god belonging only to Kapoi and his immediate household; according to Hawaiian custom any individual could select anything he wished as the god for himself and family. Kapoi's owl-god secured the aid of the king of owls, who lived in Manoa Valley on Owl's Hill, and the king of owls sent out a call for the owls of all the islands to come and make war against the king of Oahu and his warriors. Kauai legends say that the sound of the drum of the owl-king was so penetrating that it could be heard across all the channels by the owls on the different islands; in one day the owls of Hawaii, Lanai, Maui and Molokai had gathered at Kalapueo, the owls of Koolau and Kahikiku of Oahu in Kanoniakapueo, and the owls of Kauai and Niihau in Pueo-hulu-nui near Moanalua. Kakuhihewa had set apart the day of Ka-ne as the day when Kapoi should be sacrificed; in the morning of that day the priests were to slay Kapoi and place him on the altar in the presence of the king and his warriors. At daybreak the owls rallied around that temple; as the sun rose its light was obscured - the owls were clouds covering the heavens. Warriors and chiefs and priests tried to drive the birds away; the owls flew down and tore the eyes and faces of the men of Kakuhihewa, scratched dirt over them and befouled them. Such an attack was irresistible: Kakuhihewa's men fled, and Kapoi was set free. Kakuhihewa said to Kapoi: 'Your god has mana, miraculous power, greater than my god. Your god is a true god.' Kapoi was saved, the owl was worshipped as a god, and the place of that battle was Kukaeunahio-ka-pueo, the confused noise of owls rising in masses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Old Honolulu, ch. 18 (1915); not verbatim.
